item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire network security provider Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal. "The deal marks CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition to date and is among the largest in the sector as businesses consolidate and ramp up defenses to fend off AI-powered attacks," reports CNBC. "We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen."
CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open. Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge. Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion.
[...] Analysts view the Zscaler deal as a major AI security opportunity, allowing CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending and close a significant gap with Palo Alto. "The addition of ZS to CRWD's platform could bring more breadth in an era of vendor consolidation and, more importantly, network security to position the company more effectively for rising demand for AI Sovereignty," wrote analysts at JPMorgan.

item.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
President Trump reportedly directed a behind-the-scenes effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, enlisting Vice President JD Vance to secure assurances from federal officials that Huang was not facing criminal charges or considered a national security risk. According to The New York Times, the intervention came despite intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy linked to an investigation into illegal Nvidia chip shipments to China. From the report: [...] Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. On Sunday night, Nvidia's board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang's reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.
In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang's biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump's key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.
On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia's action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company "made the correct and proper decision." The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Mr. Trump wrote.

item.title: YC Startup Working On 'Cost Per Kill' For Missiles
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he's not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator's fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. "I think missiles are the coolest thing," Dandzbergs tells WIRED. "A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up."
In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about "attacking hard problems," breaking things down to "first principles," and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war -- a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. "He's a pretty exceptional person," says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. "I'm still somewhat in disbelief that we're talking about a 16-year-old." Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup's guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the "cost per kill." Dandzbergs hopes to demonstrate a prototype missile by December. Despite concerns about the ethical implications of autonomous weapons and his young age, he remains undeterred. "I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare," he says.
"Please don't say I'm sacrificing my childhood," says Dandzbergs. "This is the childhood I dreamed of."

item.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports: A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course." Clayton told CNN: "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road."
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning on CBS News' Face the Nation: "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks ... The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now."

item.title: HanLP Edges spaCy: 50 Open Source Named Entity Recognition Tools Ranked by GitHub Stars
item.author: Text Mining
item.content:encoded: HanLP (36.5K stars) edges out spaCy (34.1K) as the most-starred open source named entity recognition project on GitHub, with Flair a distant third at 14.4K. Below are all 50 NER libraries, models, datasets and labeling tools with 1,000+ stars in the Text Mining directory, ranked.Named entity recognition is one of NLP's oldest jobs: find the people, places, companies, dates and amounts in a pile of text. For a while it looked like large language models would swallow it, since you can just ask a chatbot to list the entities. Then the GLiNER paper at NAACL 2024 showed a compact bidirectional encoder beating both ChatGPT and fine-tuned LLMs on zero-shot NER benchmarks, at a fraction of the cost. The other force reshaping the category is privacy. As HackerNoon's write-up on detecting and masking personal data in text explains, PII detection is NER with a gazetteer bolted on, and that's exactly what the fastest-moving repos on this list do.The Text Mining directory tracks 7,044 open source text mining projects on GitHub. Its Named Entity Recognition filter tags 297 of them, holding about 367K stars between them. We kept repos with 1,000+ stars (67) and removed 17 that are tagged NER but aren't NER tools: general NLP courses and interview notes, paper lists, knowledge graph tutorials, pretraining frameworks and chatbot apps. That leaves 50. Star counts are from the directory's November 20, 2026 snapshot.A few patterns stand out in the full category: 201 of the 297 NER repos are Python. JavaScript (13) and Java (12) are a distant second and third.Chinese NER is a world of its own. 66 of the 297 repos describe Chinese-language work, including 16 of the top 50. Chinese has no spaces between words, so segmentation and entity recognition are usually solved together. 166 of the 297 repos haven't been pushed since before 2024. Many are BiLSTM-CRF and early BERT implementations from 2018 to 2021: still useful for learning, risky to build on. 80 of the 297 repos list no license at all, including 8 in the top 50, and CoreNLP is GPL-3.0.HanLP by hankcs: 36.5K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Multilingual NLP toolkit that's strongest in Chinese: segmentation, POS tagging, NER, dependency and semantic parsing, coreference and more.spaCy by explosion: 34.1K stars, Python, MIT. Industrial-strength Python NLP with pretrained NER pipelines for many languages. The default pick for production entity extraction.flair by flairNLP: 14.4K stars, Python, other license. Simple PyTorch framework for sequence labeling, with pretrained NER models for English, German and other languages.compromise by spencermountain: 12.2K stars, JavaScript, MIT. Lightweight JavaScript NLP that tags people, places and organizations right in the browser.presidio by data-privacy-stack: 12K stars, Python, MIT. Detects, redacts, masks and anonymizes PII across text, images and structured data.CoreNLP by stanfordnlp: 10.1K stars, Java, GPL-3.0. Stanford's Java suite for tokenization, sentence splitting, NER, parsing and coreference.stanza by stanfordnlp: 7.9K stars, Python, other license. Stanford's Python library for tokenization, NER and parsing across many human languages.DeepPavlov by deeppavlov: 7K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Open source library for dialog systems and chatbots, with NER models among its components.nlp.js by axa-group: 6.6K stars, JavaScript, MIT. NLP library for building bots, with entity extraction, sentiment analysis and language identification.openmed by maziyarpanahi: 5.8K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Local-first healthcare AI: clinical NER and HIPAA PII de-identification on hardware you control.BERT-BiLSTM-CRF-NER by macanv: 4.9K stars, Python, no license listed. TensorFlow NER using BiLSTM-CRF on top of BERT fine-tuning, with a serving setup.DeepKE by zjunlp: 4.5K stars, Python, MIT. EMNLP 2022 toolkit for knowledge graph extraction, from entities to relations and attributes.Chinese-Names-Corpus by wainshine: 4.4K stars, Other, Apache-2.0. Corpus of Chinese, Japanese and English personal names for segmentation and person-name recognition.GLiNER by urchade: 4.3K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Small bidirectional-encoder model that extracts any entity type you name, with no retraining.simpletransformers by ThilinaRajapakse: 4.3K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Wraps Hugging Face Transformers so NER, classification and QA take a few lines of code.spark-nlp by JohnSnowLabs: 4.2K stars, Scala, Apache-2.0. John Snow Labs' NLP library for Apache Spark, with pretrained NER pipelines that run at cluster scale.lac by baidu: 4K stars, C++, Apache-2.0. Baidu's lexical analysis tool for Chinese segmentation, POS tagging, NER and word importance.snips-nlu by snipsco: 4K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Python library that extracts intents and slot entities from text, built by Snips for voice assistants.Jiagu by ownthink: 3.4K stars, Python, MIT. Chinese NLP toolkit covering segmentation, POS tagging, NER, relation extraction, sentiment, keywords and summaries.pyhanlp by hankcs: 3.2K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Python interface to HanLP for Chinese segmentation and entity recognition.rust-bert by guillaume-be: 3.1K stars, Rust, Apache-2.0. Rust-native transformer pipelines, including NER, built on BERT, DistilBERT, GPT-2 and others.HarvestText by blmoistawinde: 2.6K stars, Python, MIT. Chinese text mining and preprocessing: cleaning, new-word discovery, sentiment, entity recognition and linking, keywords.Kashgari by BrikerMan: 2.4K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Transfer-learning framework on tf.keras for text labeling and classification.zh-NER-TF by Determined22: 2.3K stars, Python, no license listed. A simple BiLSTM-CRF model for Chinese NER in TensorFlow.named_entity_recognition by luopeixiang: 2.3K stars, Python, no license listed. Chinese NER implemented four ways (HMM, CRF, BiLSTM and BiLSTM+CRF), handy for learning the trade-offs.Information-Extraction-Chinese by crownpku: 2.3K stars, Python, no license listed. Chinese NER with IDCNN/BiLSTM+CRF, plus relation extraction with BiGRU and attention.BERT-NER-Pytorch by lonePatient: 2.2K stars, Python, MIT. Chinese NER with BERT using softmax, CRF and span heads.universal-data-tool by UniversalDataTool: 2.1K stars, JavaScript, MIT. Web and desktop app for labeling text, images and documents, including entity spans.sequence_tagging by guillaumegenthial: 2K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. LSTM-CRF named entity recognition in TensorFlow.NCRFpp by jiesutd: 1.9K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Neural sequence labeling toolkit for NER, POS tagging and segmentation.LatticeLSTM by jiesutd: 1.8K stars, Python, no license listed. Code for the ACL 2018 paper on Chinese NER with a lattice LSTM.Recognizers-Text by microsoft: 1.8K stars, C#, MIT. Recognizes and resolves numbers, units, dates and times in multiple languages.NeuroNER by Franck-Dernoncourt: 1.7K stars, Python, MIT. Neural network NER built to be easy to use.CLUENER2020 by CLUEbenchmark: 1.5K stars, Python, no license listed. Fine-grained Chinese NER dataset and benchmark.anago by Hironsan: 1.5K stars, Python, MIT. BiLSTM-CRF and ELMo for NER and POS tagging.ChineseNER by buppt: 1.5K stars, Python, no license listed. Chinese entity extraction with BiLSTM+CRF in TensorFlow and PyTorch.spacy-llm by explosion: 1.4K stars, Python, MIT. Plugs LLMs into spaCy pipelines, so you can prompt for entities and still get structured output.wink-nlp by winkjs: 1.4K stars, JavaScript, MIT. Developer-friendly JavaScript NLP with built-in entity recognition.natasha by natasha: 1.4K stars, Python, MIT. Basic Russian NLP, including NER for names, locations and organizations.xmnlp by SeanLee97: 1.3K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Chinese NLP: segmentation, POS tagging, NER, sentiment, spelling correction, pinyin and more.Company-Names-Corpus by wainshine: 1.3K stars, Other, Apache-2.0. Corpus of company and organization names, abbreviations and brands for organization-name recognition.rizzo-pii by Rizzo-AI-Academy: 1.3K stars, Python, MIT. Local-first privacy guard that anonymizes documents before you share them with an LLM.BERT-NER by kaiyinzhou: 1.3K stars, Python, MIT. Google's BERT applied to NER on the CoNLL-2003 dataset.BERT-NER by kamalkraj: 1.2K stars, Python, AGPL-3.0. PyTorch named entity recognition with BERT.Entity-Relation-Extraction by yuanxiaosc: 1.2K stars, Python, no license listed. Pipeline entity and relation extraction with TensorFlow and BERT, from a 2019 Chinese information extraction competition.seqeval by chakki-works: 1.2K stars, Python, MIT. Python framework for scoring NER, POS tagging and other sequence labeling output.ontogpt by monarch-initiative: 1.1K stars, Jupyter Notebook, BSD-3-Clause. LLM-based ontological extraction tools, including SPIRES.YEDDA by jiesutd: 1.1K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Lightweight collaborative text span annotation tool, nominated for ACL 2018 best demo.name-dataset by philipperemy: 1K stars, Python, Apache-2.0. Python library for names, useful as a gazetteer for person-name detection.The long tail (100 to 999 stars) is where you'll find single-language pipelines for Vietnamese, Persian, Bengali and Turkish, medical and legal entity extractors, and research code for nested and few-shot NER. Browse all 297 on the Named Entity Recognition filter, or narrow by language, license and last-updated date. item.content:encoded: "Only God and the government."That was Sara Jane Osborn's answer when someone asked who might know what she saw over Anchorage.She had been taking pictures of a rainbow in June when she spotted something unusual above a distant tree line. It looked like a dark jellyfish, so she started recording. The video lasted about three minutes and eventually went viral in November.The footage, however, left some important questions unanswered. Nobody could tell how big the object was or exactly how far away it was.A similar-looking object filmed over Iraq received a much closer examination. The Pentagon's unidentified-object office reviewed 17 minutes of footage, along with the recording details and viewing angles. Its conclusion? With moderate confidence, the object was a cluster of balloons.The difference between these two cases will allow us to examine how often we make claims in our writing without giving readers enough information to verify them.What Makes a Claim Unverifiable?The Anchorage object is what happens when there's not enough information to support a conclusion. Writers often run into a similar problem when they half-remember something they read years ago and present it as a fact.Empty claims often come disguised as convincing statements. Here are some common examples: Which studies? Who conducted them? How many people were involved? A sentence like "Studies show that waking at 5 a.m. makes people more productive" sounds solid until you ask those three questions. Which experts? Are they researchers, practitioners, or people with a large following? If you can't identify them, the statement doesn't carry much weight.Suspiciously neat statistics. "90 percent of people struggle with this" sounds like a proper statistic. But where did it come from? Who was surveyed? How many people took part? A number doesn't become evidence simply because it has a percentage sign. Best according to whom? Best for what purpose? And compared with which alternatives? Without some context, it's an empty label.Four Questions Worth Asking About Every ClaimLike the Anchorage video where we couldn’t establish the object’s size, distance, or exact position, writing articles that include claims without backed-up data makes it difficult to investigate.Here are four questions you must ask: These are statistics, productivity, percentages, increases, and other measurable claims. "A lot" and "a huge increase" are not sizes. A number alone means little and can be misleading. Saving 20 minutes a day is impressive or trivial depending on what it was before. Where did the information come from? Was it a published study, an official report, a personal observation, or something you measured yourself? "I counted" is a source. Information changes. A claim about a company's revenue, product pricing, or market share might no longer be accurate a year later.If a sentence can't answer at least the first three, it is probably a jellyfish.What It Costs You and How to Fix ItA reader who spots an unsupported statement may start questioning the entire article. Even the claims you've carefully researched can lose credibility because of one sentence you couldn't verify.The problem goes beyond individual writers, too. When there's no reliable information to establish what something is, people can attach almost any explanation to it. That's what happened with the Anchorage footage. Claims without evidence leave room for speculation, and speculation can spread quickly.So, how do you catch these problems before publishing?Start by reading your draft and highlighting every sentence that states a fact, gives a number, or explains why something happened. Then run each one through the four questions. For every one that fails, choose one of four moves. Give the number, the source, or the date. Say only what you saw. "In my case" or "among the 12 people I asked" is honest and strong. "I think" costs nothing and protects your credibility. If the article reads fine without the sentence, then take it out. Not every thought needs to make it to the final draft.Before you hit publish, go back to the boldest claim in your article and ask yourself how much? Compared with what? Says who? When? If you have the answers, include them. If you don't, make the claim smaller, present it as an opinion, or take it out altogether. Whatever you do, don't leave your readers staring at another mysterious jellyfish.Want to take this further? item.title: Team8 Expands Into AI Infrastructure With Infra Village Launch at the NYSE, Names 2027's AI Leaders
item.author: Kevin John
item.content:encoded: For large organizations, the conversation around artificial intelligence (AI) is moving past whether to adopt it and toward what it takes to run it at scale. , a venture fund with more than $2 billion in assets under management, is organizing its next phase of investing around that shift. The firm has launched the Infra Village on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), widening its company-building and investment activities to cover AI and software infrastructure.The initiative was showcased at an NYSE industry event, where Team8 also unveiled its Next AI Leaders of 2027, a recognition program created in collaboration with Amazon Web Services (AWS), Anthropic and OpenAI. The program recognizes the next generation of influential technology executives shaping how AI is built, secured and deployed.Why Team8 Is Directing Capital Toward AI InfrastructureTeam8 ties the launch to a broader shift in the AI market. As organizations move past experimentation and deploy AI across their operations, the firm says, the challenge is increasingly about the infrastructure required to run these systems with control, reliability and predictable costs.Liran Grinberg, Co-founder and Managing Partner at Team8, framed the expansion in historical terms. "Every major technology revolution eventually becomes an infrastructure revolution. AI is no exception. As enterprises move from experimentation to large-scale adoption, the companies that will define this next chapter are those solving the fundamental challenges of running AI reliably, securely, and economically," he said.Portfolio Results Behind the Infrastructure PushThe firm is not entering the category from a standing start. Team8 has already created and backed several infrastructure companies, including Port, Finout and Classiq, which it counts among the fastest-growing companies in its portfolio.Grinberg tied the new effort directly to the firm's resources and relationships. "We see an opportunity to apply our company-building experience, capital, and enterprise network to help create the next generation of infrastructure companies," he said.How the Infra Village Is StructuredThe Infra Village combines three elements: a dedicated venture-creation effort, additional investments and a new executive-village community. Together they are meant to help build the infrastructure layer that the next generation of enterprise AI will rely on, a foundation that Team8 describes as spanning compute, inference, data, developer platforms, observability and security.The community component follows a format Team8 has used before. Israel became a global cybersecurity powerhouse by combining deep technical talent with early, direct access to the enterprises defining the industry's most pressing challenges, and Team8 helped develop that model through its CISO Village, which connected cybersecurity founders with enterprise security leaders, including chief information security officers (CISOs). The Infra Village extends the same Village model to AI and software infrastructure. Chief information officers (CIOs), chief technology officers (CTOs) and AI and infrastructure executives from major enterprises gain a vendor-neutral setting to discuss what works in production, how infrastructure costs are developing and which technology investments deserve attention. The same community gives founders direct connections to those executives.Aviad Harell, Managing Partner at Team8, explained the thinking behind the community. "Building successful infrastructure companies starts with understanding the problems enterprises are facing in production. The Infra Village brings the executives responsible for these decisions into direct conversation with the founders developing the solutions," he said. "By creating a vendor-neutral environment for sharing knowledge and identifying emerging needs, we can help founders build companies around real enterprise challenges and accelerate the development of the AI infrastructure ecosystem."A Faster Decision Cycle for Enterprise Technology SpendingTeam8 also points to the pace of change. Decisions that once took years are now being made within a single quarter, according to the firm, and responsibility for AI infrastructure is spread across CIOs, CTOs and data leaders rather than sitting with one owner. The vendor landscape is also changing faster than traditional analyst cycles. At the same time, the capabilities behind enterprise AI must support workloads that did not exist just three years ago, while helping organizations manage environments that are becoming more complex and more expensive.Team8 sees this transition as an opportunity to apply its established company-building model to a new category of enterprise technology. The Infra Village brings the CIOs, CTOs and infrastructure executives responsible for these decisions into direct contact with the founders building solutions.The Next AI Leaders of 2027The Next AI Leaders of 2027 program was created in collaboration with AWS, HumanX, NYSE, Kiteworks, Goodwin, Meitar and Anthropic, according to Team8. Judges include senior industry experts such as Erwan Menard, SVP Product Management, Crusoe; Tasso Argyros, VP of Engineering, Databricks; Apoorv Jha, Applied AI, OpenAI; Andrew Blum, Co-Founder & COO, HumanX; Rachael Wang, Head of Agentic AI Professional Services, AWS; and Andrew Reiskind, Chief Data Officer, Mastercard. Selected from hundreds of nominations, the 20 honorees include CIOs, CTOs and senior technology executives, many of whom already lead AI infrastructure initiatives at major organizations. Their work spans AI infrastructure and compute, inference, developer platforms, data and applied AI, at organizations including Microsoft, Meta, Adobe, Anthropic, Salesforce, Cloudflare, CoreWeave, Cerebras, Mistral AI and Wiz, among others.Andy Parsons, Global Head of Content Authenticity, AdobeBarak Yagour, VP of Engineering, MetaDaniel Marcous, Co-Founder & Chief Builder (CPTO), aprilEmily Capodilupo, SVP of Research, Algorithms, and Data, WHOOPHeather McGeory, VP, Energy & Sustainability, CoreWeaveInna Weiner, VP Product, Data, AI and Cloud Platform, AppsFlyerJared Palmer, VP of Engineering, CognitionKatelyn Lesse, Head of Platform Engineering, AnthropicMahadev Konar, SVP Infrastructure Engineering, Together AINancy Zheng, VP, AI Inference, CerebrasNidhi Chappell, President of AI Infrastructure, NscaleRazik Yousfi, SVP & GM, AI Products, Tempus AIRita Kozlov, VP Product, Developer Platform & AI, CloudflareRotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily (a Nebius company)Sesh Nalla, VP of Engineering & Research, DatadogShir Chorev, Co-Founder & CTO, Deepchecks (now part of Check Point)Solal Raveh, CTO of Product Infrastructure, Wiz (now part of Google Cloud)Stefana Muller, VP of Engineering, SalesforceYann Leger, VP Cloud Compute, Mistral AIYitzhak Kesselman, Corporate Vice President, Microsoft Fabric, MicrosoftTeam8 positions the Infra Village as the next step in carrying its venture creation and investment models, its network of industry leaders and its company validation process into the infrastructure that powers enterprise AI. The firm's stated aim is to position founders to address some of the world's most significant technology challenges, starting with the systems enterprises need to run AI at scale.

item.title: Thinking Inertia: Stanford Researchers Find LLMs Keep Reasoning Even When Told to Stop Thinking
item.author: Cognizance
item.content:encoded: Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To Dianqiao Lei, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Pan Lu, Philip Torr, James Zou (Stanford University)Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly ship with explicit “thinking modes”, yet their counterpart, “no-thinking”, has received far less attention. In this work, we study LLMs’ “no-thinking” behavior along two axes. a. How to measure no-thinking? Prior work typically defines no-thinking through proxies such as a disabled thinking mode or the absence of long traces. These proxies are unreliable: disabled thinking modes still emit extended reasoning, or long traces often contain uninformative filler rather than genuine inference. We instead normalize any LLM response into pre-answer trace and a final answer, and evaluate it at three levels: (i) an Empty-Thinking Rate for strict answer-only compliance; (ii) an instruction-aware Question–Pre-answer Relevance to calculate similarity between question and pre-answer trace; and (iii) an additional LLM-as-judge Explicit Inference Rate for visible explicit inference. Together, these levels separate answer-only output, relevant but non-inferential text, and explicit inference. Human studies demonstrate the effectiveness of these metrics. b. How does no-thinking vary across tasks and models? We evaluate six prompting intervention settings on six widely used LLMs (both open-source and commercial models) across three question types: Boolean, multiple-choice, and open-ended. We find that explicit no-think controls cannot reliably eliminate visible explicit inference; models instead exhibit : visible explicit inference persists even under strict no-thinking controls, and becomes progressively more prevalent as the answer space opens; On the another hand, accuracy remains relatively stable on Boolean and multiple-choice tasks, whereas open-ended tasks expose a trade-off between answer-only compliance and task accuracy. Finally, rewriting the same questions across answer spaces shows that supplying candidate answers makes answer-only responses substantially easier to produce. Taken together, these findings establish no-thinking as a non-trivial capability of LLMs: stopping explicit reasoning cannot be assumed from model settings or instructions alone, and deserves systematic evaluation alongside reasoning ability itself.Figure 1: No-thinking controls do not guarantee response-level no-thinking. (Left) On a representative MMLU question, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3-235B-A22B are asked for only the final option, yet expose question-relevant pre-answer text. Appendix Figure E.1 confirms the instruction’s clear answer-only reading. Under native no-thinking, green ETR and orange visible-length bars across the six benchmarks show Boolean tasks closer to answer-only than multiple-choice and open-ended tasks.LLMs have benefited substantially from extended reasoning. From early chain-of-thought prompting [42, 19] to more recent test-time scaling [31, 3], allocating additional tokens to intermediate computation before returning an answer has significantly improved performance across a wide range of tasks. The same mechanism, however, raises inference cost in both latency and token consumption, motivating a line of work on shortening, budgeting, or compressing reasoning traces [1, 18, 11, 45]. Beyond efficiency, knowing when to answer directly without extended reasoning is also important for human-like adaptive reasoning: humans often respond from intuition and deliberate only when needed. Together, these efficiency and adaptivity considerations motivate explicit control over reasoning behavior. As illustrated in Figure 2 (a), current frontier systems expose native thinking switches and reasoning-effort settings, while users can request direct answers through prompting [25, 46, 8].Figure 2: Surface proxies fail to identify response-level no-thinking. (a) Three common proxies: 1. prompt-side control, 2. special reasoning tokens (e.g.,), and 3. generation token length. On the same algebra question, disabling the thinking mode, omitting special thinking tokens, or producing a short output can each leave a visible inferential step before the final answer. These cases motivate separately evaluating strict answer-only compliance, pre-answer relevance, and visible explicit inference.Despite these explicit controls, as Figure 2 (b) illustrates, a frontier model with its reasoning channel disabled can still emit question-conditioned content in the ordinary answer channel or produce a short response that nonetheless contains a compact, task-specific reasoning step. Moreover, the community still lacks a clear definition of what a “no-thinking” response should look like. In practice, no-thinking is typically inferred from surface proxies: the prompt is placed in a no-think regime [22]; the response does not return a separate reasoning trace, or the block is absent [46, 8]; or the output is simply short [1, 18, 11, 24, 45]. These proxies conflate instruction control with the suppression of visible reasoning. For example, a generic lead-in such as “Let me think about this. The answer should be ” carries no task-specific content, yet would be counted as reasoning by surface proxies. Conversely, a single compact equation may expose an explicit inferential step even when the response is short or contains no special reasoning tokens.Motivated by this conflation, we study no-thinking as an observable response behavior and inspect the pre-answer text exposed before the final answer. (Footnote: Here, no-thinking is used as a response-level concept, distinct from latent reasoning processes within the LLM.) In general question answering, pre-answer text may reflect reasoning, paraphrasing, fact restatement, or simple assertion. We therefore define three progressively more specific criteria for characterizing such text. a view of whether the complete visible output reaches the strict answer-only boundary, measured by the Empty-Thinking Rate (ETR); a view of whether any remaining pre-answer text T is relevant to the question Q, measured by instruction-aware Qwen3-Embedding-4B via Question–Pre-answer Relevance (QRel.); and a view of whether T contains an explicit inferential step that addresses Q, measured by a blinded GPT-5.5 judge through the Explicit Inference Rate (EIR). The judge separates explicit inference from paraphrases and relevant non-inferential text, while task accuracy independently evaluates the final answer A. Thus, QRel. provides a relevance signal rather than final evidence of reasoning; conclusions about visible reasoning and thinking inertia rely on EIR together with ETR. This view defines a testable behavioral framework for comparing interventions, benchmarks, model families, and model scales.Based on these metrics, our experiments further examine whether no-thinking can be controlled, regularized, and generalized. We first ask whether enabling or disabling the thinking mode actually suppresses visible pre-answer content. We then compare several interventions (Footnote: We use to denote a controlled change to the model’s thinking configuration, the output constraints, or the question’s answer interface.) to test whether stronger answer-only constraints can make responses more answer-only without damaging task accuracy. Finally, we evaluate how this behavior changes across answer spaces, benchmark domains, and LLMs of different families and scales. The detailed intervention spectrum is introduced in Section 2.4; at a high level, it separates native no-think behavior, reasoning re-elicitation, semantic suppression, and structural prefix forcing. Our human validation supports all three metrics: a manual boundary audit corroborates ETR, the five annotators’ relevance judgments align closely with QRel., and their explicit-inference labels achieve 98.8% mean binary agreement with the primary GPT-5.5 judge used to compute EIR. The human annotations also reproduce the main answer-space and intervention trends, further supporting our central conclusions. The EIR results also remain robust when evaluated by an independent judge from a different model family.Our results highlight four findings. Explicit no-think controls are not reliable no-thinking controls: even a frontier LLM such as DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) retains visible explicit inference in 99.9% of open-ended responses under its disabled-thinking setting. LLMs exhibit : visible inference is organized more by the task’s answer space than by the switch itself. Under both native and strict no-thinking settings, it remains lowest on Boolean tasks, intermediate on multiple-choice tasks, and highest on open-ended tasks. On open-ended tasks, stronger answer-only instructions reveal what we call a no-thinking–performance trade-off: stronger suppression improves answer-only compliance and reduces visible inference, but can also reduce task accuracy. Specifically, across the five LLMs with fully disabled thinking, strict answer-only prompting raises mean ETR from near zero to roughly 40% while reducing mean accuracy by about 15 percentage points. Answer space matters: for the same question, fact-like and candidate-visible formats make answer-only responses easier to produce than open-generation formats, showing that the pattern is not explained by benchmark difficulty or answer length alone.In summary, our work makes two contributions. First, we define no-thinking as a measurable response-level behavior and provide a framework for evaluating it. Second, through comprehensive experiments across task families and diverse LLMs, we identify systematic behaviors including thinking inertia, the no-thinking–performance trade-off, and answer-space dependence. Together, these contributions support the broader goal of developing LLMs that, like humans, can adaptively determine when to reason and when to answer directly.No-thinking in LLMs does not have a concrete definition. In practice, existing work often identifies it through three surface proxies, as summarized on the left side of Figure 2: () , where the model is run in a no-think setting or is not prompted to think step by step [22]; () , where no-thinking is inferred from the absence of an explicit block or a separate reasoning trace [46, 8]; and () , where shorter generations produced by length control or chain-of-thought compression are treated as reduced reasoning [1, 18]. These proxies are convenient and easy to monitor, but they characterize the response by its surface prompting condition, visible format, or length, rather than by the actual content of the LLM response (such as the question-conditioned information it actually exposes).Each of these formulations, however, has a simple failure case, illustrated on the right side of Figure 2. () A no-think instruction can still yield explanatory, question-dependent text before the final answer; disabling a thinking mode therefore does not by itself remove visible reasoning. () Removing explicit tags only removes a particular format; reasoning may still appear as ordinary language in the answer channel. () Making an output short does not make it no-thinking, since a compact response can still encode the essential intermediate step needed to answer the question. Thus, the problem is not that these proxies are useless, but that none of them defines the behavioral object we want to study. We therefore operationalize no-thinking at the response level and progressively distinguish strict answer-only compliance, question relevance, and visible explicit inference. This observable definition does not make claims about latent computation inside the model, because extending the analysis to latent reasoning would substantially broaden the scope and make the boundary of no-thinking difficult to define clearly.Figure 3: Response-centric metrics for measuring no-thinking. Top: the LLM inference process. A question Q is wrapped by an intervention S⁡(⋅) to form the model input S⁡(Q), which the model π maps to a response decomposed into pre-answer text T and final answer A. We evaluate the visible response through three levels: strict answer-only compliance (ETR), question–pre-answer relevance (QRel.), and LLM judge explicit inference (EIR); accuracy independently evaluates A. six representative response cases to the same question “42+79=?” vary in length, relevance, and inferential content while sharing the same final answer. Case 1 is answer-only (empty T), whereas Cases 2–6 use the non-empty-T labels from the mutually exclusive rubric in Table 1: Cases 2 and 4 are explicit reasoning, Cases 3 and 5 are generic/off-topic, and Case 6 is relevant non-inferential. Table 1 additionally defines paraphrase-only and unclear; representative real outputs are provided in Appendix F.1.The observations above suggest that prompt-side heuristics alone are insufficient for studying no-thinking in a controlled way. We therefore ground our analysis in the response-centric framework shown in Figure 3.Formally, let π denote a language model and Q a task sample. The query is wrapped by an intervention S⁡(⋅) ( a system prompt such as “please answer directly”) before being passed to the model, which produces an observable response\pi\bigl(S(Q)\bigr)=\left(T,A\right) where A is the last parseable final answer and T comprises all readable visible text preceding it. We use (T,A) only as a decomposition of the observable response, without making claims about task-relevant computation in unobserved model states. The strict compliance check additionally scans the complete output, so substantive text after A is not treated as answer-only. Appendix E audits question restatement and answer-first edge cases.Visible pre-answer text T. T contains all readable visible content before the final answer A, whether it appears in a special reasoning block, the ordinary answer channel, or a short lead-in. It may include an explicit derivation, a compact reasoning step, a paraphrase, a relevant assertion, or a generic template such as “The answer is”. These cases motivate evaluating the content of T rather than equating every non-empty T with reasoning.Question type and answer space (Q,A). We write each task sample as , where q is the question, c is optional context, and is the admissible answer space, with . For example, \mathcal{A}=\{\texttt{yes},\texttt{no}\} for Boolean verification, \mathcal{A}=\{\texttt{A},\texttt{B},\texttt{C},\texttt{D}\} for multiple-choice, and permits free-form generation for open-ended tasks. This lets us test whether no-thinking behavior changes under different answer interfaces. S⁡(⋅) denotes an external intervention applied to Q before generation, producing the model input S⁡(Q). We consider two broad classes: () question-irrelevant interventions, which change the instruction, output constraint, or explicit thinking configuration while keeping Q fixed ( prepending “Answer directly without thinking”); and () question-relevant interventions, which modify the task instance itself, such as its surface form or answer space ( converting an open-ended question into a multiple-choice one).Together, this unified framework allows us to study no-thinking through strict compliance, relevance, and explicit inference rather than through surface proxies alone.2.3 Three-Level Response EvaluationUnder our formulation, T serves as the primary observable target, while task accuracy separately evaluates the final answer A. We therefore organize the T measurement into three progressively more specific levels (as depicted in Figure 3): strict answer-only compliance, pre-answer relevance, and visible explicit inference. At the response level, Levels 1 and 3 yield binary scores, whereas Level 2 yields a continuous score; their benchmark-level aggregates are defined below.Level 1: Empty-Thinking Rate. We first ask whether each output is strictly answer-only. For output i, let ei denote the response-level empty-thinking indicator. For a benchmark with N outputs under a fixed model and intervention, we define the response-level score and the Empty-Thinking Rate (ETR) ase_{i}=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{|T_{i}|=0\right\},\qquad\mathrm{ETR}=100\%\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e_{i}. Here, ei is the response-level score, whereas ETR is its benchmark-level rate. Operationally, ei=1 only when Ai is parseable and the complete visible output contains no substantive text outside its permitted answer wrapper; otherwise, ei=0. Thus, empty Ti does not override a malformed final-answer format, and substantive text following Ai also violates strict compliance. ETR gives the cleanest operational limit, but cannot distinguish a generic template, a paraphrase, and a question-specific inference once Ti is non-empty.Level 2: Question–Pre-answer Relevance. We next ask how strongly the visible pre-answer text T is semantically related to Q. Let ϕ denote an embedding encoder. We instantiate ϕ with the instruction-aware Qwen3-Embedding-4B [50], because its query instruction lets us specify the intended relation between Q and T: Q is encoded as the query under the instruction “Given a question, retrieve pre-answer text that contains reasoning relevant to answering the question,” while T is encoded as the candidate passage. Here, ϕ⁡(Q) denotes the resulting instruction-conditioned query embedding and ϕ⁡(T) the candidate-passage embedding produced by the same encoder. After ℓ2-normalizing each embedding, i.e., dividing each vector by its Euclidean norm, we define the response-level Question–Pre-answer Relevance (QRel.) score as\mathrm{QRel.}(Q_{i},T_{i})=\begin{cases}0,&|T_{i}|=0,\\ \cos\!\bigl(\phi(Q_{i}),\phi(T_{i})\bigr),&|T_{i}|>0.\end{cases} The first branch assigns empty Ti a score of zero, while the second directly uses the cosine similarity for non-empty Ti. For each model–benchmark–intervention setting, the reported QRel. is the arithmetic mean of these response-level scores over all N outputs, including the zeros assigned to empty Ti. The instruction-aware objective makes relevance to answering Qi, rather than surface overlap alone, the target relation.However, QRel. measures relevance rather than inference: a paraphrase or a relevant answer assertion can receive a high score without containing an inferential step. Appendix E audits whether near-verbatim or semantic restatement drives the aggregate results, while Level 3 keeps such text outside the explicit-inference category.Level 3: Explicit Inference Rate. Level 1 checks a structural rule and Level 2 measures functional relevance; neither directly separates reasoning from relevant non-inferential text. We therefore use a blinded LLM judge to classify each non-empty Ti. The judge receives only (Qi,Ti); model identity, intervention mode, final answer Ai, correctness, and QRel. are hidden. It returns one of the five mutually exclusive labels in Table 1, together with an exact supporting span from Ti. The span records the evidence for the selected label and makes the decision auditable, but does not enter the metric. Table 1 presents the judge instruction and rubric together.Generic lead-in, formatting text, or off-topic content with no question-specific inference.Restates Q or supplied facts without connecting them through an inference step.Gives a relevant fact, definition, description, or answer assertion without an inference step.Contains deduction, computation, comparison, elimination, rule application, evidence-to-conclusion, or causality addressing Q.Cannot be classified reliably from the visible text.Table 1: Blinded LLM-judge instruction and rubric for non-empty pre-answer text T. Empty T is handled separately and counts as no visible explicit inference.A relevant restatement or answer assertion alone is therefore not reasoning, whereas one concrete inferential step can qualify even when it is short, shallow, or ultimately incorrect. For the metric, let Judge⁡(Qi,Ti) denote the binary score induced by the five-way label returned when the blinded judge receives (Qi,Ti): it is 1 only when the judge selects , and 0 for the other four labels. Empty Ti is not sent to the judge and is assigned Judge⁡(Qi,Ti)=0 by defacult. For a benchmark with N outputs under a fixed model and intervention, we define the Explicit Inference Rate (EIR) as\mathrm{EIR}=100\%\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\operatorname{Judge}(Q_{i},T_{i}). Thus, Judge⁡(Qi,Ti) is the response-level binary score, whereas EIR is its benchmark-level statistics.We complement the automated evaluation with a blinded human study that considers two aspects: , whether the three metrics align with human judgments; and , whether the main conclusions drawn from them persist under direct human annotation. A manual boundary audit checks the strict visible boundary underlying ETR, while five annotators independently provide graded relevance judgments for comparison with QRel. and explicit-inference labels for comparison with the Level 3 judge. Additionally, we use a second LLM judge from a different model family to check that the Level 3 results are not specific to the primary judge. Additionally, we use a second LLM judge from a different model family to check that the Level 3 results are not specific to the primary judge. (ii) Conclusion validation. Building on this agreement, we test whether the main answer-space and intervention trends persist under direct human annotation. The detailed protocol and results are reported in Section 3.6 and Appendix D.3.2.4 Thinking Behavior ControlTo systematically cover the possible setups, we design a six-mode spectrum (Table 2) that organizes modes along a single axis of , ranging from (−) for thinking-encouraging modes and (0) for the native no-thinking mode to (+++) for the strongest suppression. All modes share the same task stem and final-answer request; only the thinking switch and the question-irrelevant intervention change.Purpose (no-think intensity)Question-Irrelevant Intervention S⁡(⋅)Native mode (−)Native mode (0)“A very short lead-in is allowed, but do not explain.”Strict regularization (++)“Give the final answer directly without any reasoning.”Table 2: Six-mode question-irrelevant prompt intervention spectrum. Modes shown in gray (Think-On, CoT) still elicit thinking behavior and serve as thinking-side references; the remaining modes (Think-Off, Soft, Strict, Prefix) form the no-think intervention space, ranging from the native no-thinking baseline to increasingly strong semantic suppression. (Think-On, CoT). Think-On (M1) keeps the official thinking interface enabled, while CoT (M3) disables it but adds the instruction to re-elicit reasoning in the ordinary answer channel. Both elicit thinking rather than suppress it, and serve as opposite-direction references for the no-think space (gray rows in Table 2). (Think-Off, Soft, Strict, Prefix). Think-Off (M2) disables without any additional output-side control, serving as the natural baseline against which all suppression interventions are measured. Soft (M4) and Strict (M5) keep and add increasingly strong natural-language constraints: Soft allows a short lead-in but forbids explanation, while Strict asks for the answer directly without any reasoning. Prefix (M6) is qualitatively different. Instead of adding an instruction, it pre-fills the answer template “The answer is ” at the start of generation, bypassing the instruction-following channel entirely. We treat it as a separate branch rather than a stronger version of Strict.We organize our experiments around three questions. Starting from the model’s native thinking controls, we ask whether enabling or disabling the thinking mode actually suppresses visible pre-answer content. We then focus on the native no-thinking mode and ask how prompt interventions of varying strength affect no-thinking behavior and its relationship with task performance. The same annotations reproduce the answer-space staircase and persistent visible inference on Open-ended tasks under M5.Efficient and Adaptive Reasoning.Test-time computation can substantially improve language-model reasoning [31, 3], motivating methods that allocate this computation more selectively. One line of work controls the length or budget of visible reasoning through length-conditioned reinforcement learning [1], token-budget prompting [11], budget forcing [23], and self-training for concise traces [24]. Another compresses intermediate reasoning by distilling shorter chains [18] or using terse drafts [45]; a recent survey provides a broader taxonomy [32]. Empirical studies further show that more reasoning is not uniformly beneficial: unnecessarily long traces can impair efficiency and even accuracy on simple problems, while the useful reasoning length depends on both task difficulty and model capability [4, 43, 49]. Recent methods therefore train models to decide whether extended reasoning is needed [9, 47, 16, 34]. Selective reasoning has also been studied in vision-language models [36, 21].Our scope differs from optimizing the amount of test-time computation. We ask whether a requested no-thinking state is realized in the , following the common think/no-think focus on exposed CoT or reasoning channels rather than unverifiable latent cognition. We disable provider thinking interfaces or impose answer-only formats, then separately measure strict answer-only compliance, pre-answer relevance, and visible explicit inference. This distinction matters because intermediate computation need not be expressed in natural language, as demonstrated by latent-reasoning methods such as Coconut [12], and because a visible CoT need not faithfully reflect the computation that produced an answer [35, 20]. Recent work also studies whether concealed reasoning can be reconstructed or exposed. Trace Inversion synthesizes distillation-useful reasoning traces from black-box inputs, answers, and optional summaries without access to hidden CoT [48]. Encrypted reasoning blocks exposed by proprietary APIs can also be transferred to weaker models within the same provider and decoded into plaintext [27]. Prompt repetition offers a complementary input-side technique for improving non-reasoning models and evaluates final-answer accuracy, length, and latency [22]. It does not ask whether visible question-conditioned text remains, nor does it distinguish paraphrases and relevant assertions from inference. Our contribution instead decomposes the response into pre-answer text and the final answer and evaluates input- and output-side interventions through ETR, QRel., EIR, task accuracy, and same-question answer-space controls.Instruction following also underpins our intervention spectrum: the “no-think,” “answer-only,” and prefix-forcing modes are all instructions whose effectiveness depends on how reliably models obey natural-language constraints. Instruction tuning [41, 30, 5] and human-feedback alignment [26, 2] train models to follow open-ended directives, while self-generated and synthetic instruction data [39, 33] broaden the instruction distribution. Verifiable-instruction benchmarks such as IFEval [51] and FollowBench [17] evaluate compliance with output-format and content constraints, and related benchmarks study model behavior under complex or multi-constraint instructions [13, 28]. Our work uses this perspective in a targeted way: we treat “produce no reasoning” as one such verifiable output constraint, and study whether surface compliance actually removes visible question-conditioned payload rather than only matching the requested format.5 Discussion and ConclusionWe argue that “no-thinking” in LLMs should be evaluated as a response-level property rather than inferred from surface proxies such as missing reasoning tags, no-think settings, or short generations. By decomposing each output into pre-answer text T and final answer A, we progressively measure strict answer-only compliance, pre-answer relevance, and visible explicit inference, while task accuracy evaluates A independently. Across local Qwen3 models, scaled variants, and frontier APIs, we find that explicit no-think controls do not reliably remove visible explicit inference; models exhibit “” organized by answer space; stronger answer-only constraints reveal a no-thinking–performance trade-off between compliance and accuracy; and compressibility is governed by the structural support of the question itself, not by question difficulty or model capability alone. These findings suggest that building LLMs that can stop thinking on demand requires more than hiding reasoning traces or enforcing shorter outputs: it requires evaluating when direct answering is actually supported by the task.5.1 Scope and LimitationsOur analysis deliberately takes the as its unit of study. This choice provides a common behavioral basis across local models and proprietary APIs whose internal computation is neither equally exposed nor directly comparable. Our claims therefore concern visible output, not the absence of task-relevant computation from hidden states; provider signals are incorporated when available without treating them as equivalent descriptions of internal reasoning.Our six-model, six-benchmark suite is designed to isolate answer-space structure under deterministic decoding whenever supported. Generalization to multilingual, code, tool-use, multi-turn, and stochastic settings, as well as robustness to evolving proprietary endpoints, remains open. QRel. is an operational relevance complement to the exact ETR boundary rather than a standalone reasoning detector. EIR directly separates explicit inference from paraphrases and relevant non-inferential text, but remains dependent on the visible-text rubric and judge calibration; Appendix D tests this dependence with an independent judge family, and Appendix E audits near-verbatim copying, semantic paraphrases, and response order. These boundaries delimit the claims while preserving a reproducible, provider-agnostic basis for studying no-thinking.5.2 Implications and Future WorkNo-thinking is a distinct controllable capability rather than the default complement of a reasoning mode. Direct answering depends on answer-space support and computational necessity rather than on a switch or model scale alone. This suggests task-aware routing: answer directly when the interface provides sufficient support, and preserve explicit computation when suppression would sacrifice accuracy. Visible compliance should not, however, be equated with lower inference cost when hidden reasoning may remain active.One direction is to train models for calibrated stopping rather than uniform suppression, jointly optimizing accuracy, answer-only compliance, visible relevance and inference, latency, and actual reasoning-token cost. Extensions across languages and interactive tasks can test generality, while internal-state analyses can examine whether computation disappears, moves to a hidden channel, or is only omitted from view. In high-stakes settings, concise outputs may reduce cost and disclosure, but explanations remain important for verification and error detection. item.content:encoded: On November 3, American voters faced 41 local ballot measures about data centers across ten states. They favored limiting them in about 40 of the 41. Five were outright bans. In Perry, Ohio a financial-guarantee requirement passed with more than 87% of the vote. In Granville it was 84%. Ashville voted to block a campus that was already under construction.The obvious reading is that AI just lost a political fight, and that the fight will now be settled in Washington by whichever party is in charge.I think that reading is wrong in three separate ways, and the third one is the only part that matters if you build things.It is not a partisan fightGallup asked for the first time in March and found 71% oppose a data center near them, with majorities opposed in every single party group. Strongly opposed ran 56% among Democrats, 48% among independents, 39% among Republicans. For scale, 53% oppose a local nuclear plant. Data centers now poll worse than nuclear power.The structure underneath is stranger than the toplines. Heatmap’s project-level data finds roughly 55% of opposed projects sit in red, sparsely populated areas, with opposed projects in Republican places up more than 300% in six months. Republican primary voters in 2026 removed pro-data-center Republicans in Calvert County, Maryland, Box Elder County, Utah, and Spartanburg County, South Carolina.Meanwhile the officials who actually stopped statewide moratoriums were Democrats. Maine’s governor vetoed one. Michigan’s opposes the bills. New York’s declined to sign the one her legislature passed.Whatever this is, no partisan variable predicts it. If you are modeling your siting risk off which party controls a chamber, you are modeling the wrong thing.It is probably not your electricity bill eitherThis is where most of the commentary goes wrong, and where I nearly went wrong myself.The affordability anger in this election was real. It was mostly not about electricity. The September CPI shows gasoline up 34.2% and fuel oil up 74.2% year over year, against electricity at 4.4%, in a year dominated by an oil shock. The national exit poll contained no question about electricity or utility bills at all.The geography makes the point harder. Two-year residential price changes through August 2026 run about , but the increases cluster in the PJM footprint: DC +38.8%, Maine +30.1%, Illinois +19.3%, Pennsylvania +18.6%, Virginia +18.0%, Ohio +16.7%. Now look at the biggest data center states outside PJM. Texas, with roughly 474 GW of large load in its interconnection queue, about 90% of it data centers, came in at +6.5%, below the national average. Georgia +7.1%. Arizona +2.0%. California fell.Geography tracks market structure, not data center density. And the best national statistical work, from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, finds that between 2019 and 2025 states with higher load growth generally saw real retail prices fall, not rise.Do not overcorrect, though. In PJM specifically the case is strong and comes from PJM’s own independent market monitor, which re-cleared the actual auctions with the actual offers and attributed $29.4 billion of $63.6 billion in capacity charges across four auctions, about 46%, to data center load, concluding that the 2025/26 auction was “not competitive.” A separate Dallas Fed working paper models the national wholesale effect at 6.9% by 2025, and does not estimate how much of that reaches a household bill. That monitor also proposes the remedy, which is worth knowing when you read its number. The fair summary is that this is a regional capacity-market problem that became a national story.The thing that actually happenedWhile everyone argued about moratoriums, almost none were enacted. Sixteen states considered outright bans. What did become law is duller and far more consequential. Nine states passed ratepayer-protection rules in 2025 and 2026, signed by governors of both parties: Oregon, Texas, Minnesota, South Dakota, Florida, Tennessee, Oklahoma, New Jersey and California. Consultancy E3 counts 38 new large-load tariffs since 2018, 30 of them in 2025 and 2026 alone.They mostly do the same thing. If you are a very large electricity customer, you get your own rate class, and you must commit to paying for most of the capacity you reserve whether or not you use it, for ten to fourteen years.Ohio went first. The AEP Ohio tariff, approved in July 2025, covers loads above 25 MW and requires payment for at least 85% of subscribed capacity for twelve years.Here is the result, and it is the most interesting number in this entire story.By February 2026, AEP had 5,642 MW of data center load signed under the tariff. And its load forecast came in than its previous submission, a drop the utility attributes to the tariff itself.More demand disappeared than signed up.Most of the demand was never realThat number is not an anomaly. It is a measurement of something the industry has known informally for two years and rarely says out loud.Grid Strategies found that utility data center forecasts filed with FERC ran roughly 40% above credible industry projections through 2030. Aterio counted 3,969 announced US data centers against 802 under construction. Bernstein estimates only about 35% of announced North American capacity will ever be built. JPMorgan found roughly 60% of capacity planned for 2027 completion had not broken ground.The mechanism is not mysterious. When an interconnection request is free, you file several, in several states, and keep your options open. Developers were not lying. They were doing what anyone does with a free option. The tariff did not suppress demand. It priced the option, and most of the option holders walked.This is why “data centers are being blocked” is a bad description of 2026. A project that evaporates when asked for a twelve-year commitment was not a project. It was a placeholder.Meanwhile the real buildout is at a recordHere is the part that gets no coverage at all, and it is the reason I am not writing a doom piece.CBRE counted 7,481 MW under construction across eight major North American markets in the first half of 2026, about 25% more than a year earlier. Construction set a record in the same months opposition peaked. Approvals kept happening in the very jurisdictions passing restrictions. Coweta County, Georgia approved a $17 billion campus in April and passed a moratorium in June.Both things are true. The speculative queue is collapsing and the real buildout is accelerating. Those are not in tension. They are the same event seen from two sides, which is what a filter looks like while it runs.The useful translation for anyone building on this infrastructure is that the governing question changed, quietly, from a political one to a financial one.It used to be: will they let us build here. It is now: can this load pay for its own power under a decade-long take-or-pay commitment. That is a capital structure question. It has an answer, it can be modeled, and it does not depend on an election.Three things follow. Site by market structure rather than by headline incentives, because the states advertising the loudest subsidies are not the states with the cheapest marginal power. Assume you will be asked to commit, because thirty of the thirty-eight large-load tariffs arrived in the last two years and the direction is one-way. And read the collapsing queue as competitive information rather than as bad news, because when your rivals’ announced gigawatts evaporate on contact with a contract, the capacity picture you are planning against was never the real one.I run AI workloads every day across my own systems and nothing I do approaches this scale. But the shape of the lesson is the same one I keep running into and wrote about in October: when something is free to produce, people produce enormous quantities of it, and the quantity tells you nothing until someone attaches a price.Announced megawatts were free to produce. Now they are not.The part I would watch nextTwo real uncertainties. Results from November 3 were unofficial and uncertified when I wrote this, with roughly nineteen House seats and two Senate races still uncalled. And poll numbers on data centers swing hugely on wording: the 63% to 75% opposition range is for a facility “near where I live,” while POLITICO asked about one within three miles and got 37% support against 28% opposition.But the direction is not ambiguous. Nine states, both parties, thirty tariffs in two years, a flipped utility commission in Georgia, and a federal preemption order whose own Section 8 declines to touch state data-center regulation. Siting and retail rates are state powers, and the states are using them.Nobody voted to stop AI. They voted to stop paying for it.

item.title: The Truth Behind Those 100x Faster AI Chip Headlines
item.author: TheLLMSeeker
item.content:encoded: I’ve now had a version of this conversation enough times that I could write the reply in advance. Someone forwards a headline about a chip that “computes with light instead of electrons” and is supposedly a hundred times faster than an Nvidia GPU, and the message attached is always some version of “wait, is this the quantum computer thing?” From the slightly more technical friends, it’s “isn’t this just fiber optics?” Neither is a dumb question. The best-known machines that compute with photons right now are quantum computers, with companies like PsiQuantum and Xanadu building their qubits out of light. And the photonics most people have actually touched is the fiber and optical transceivers that already shuttle data between servers in every large data center. So when a startup shows up talking about lasers, waveguides, and beating Nvidia, there are two ready-made boxes waiting for it.It fits neither one. A photonic AI accelerator has no qubits, no superposition, no dilution refrigerator. It runs at room temperature, and the serious designs are built with the same CMOS-compatible manufacturing that makes ordinary chips. And it isn’t just moving data from one place to another; the light is doing the arithmetic. What it is instead is narrower and stranger than either guess, and explaining that difference is most of this post.Strip a neural network down to what the hardware actually spends its time on, and you find one operation, repeated endlessly: multiplying a vector by a matrix. A GPU does that by pushing electrons through billions of transistors, one clock cycle at a time. A photonic processor does it by letting light do the multiplying. The input numbers are encoded into the intensity or phase of light, the model’s weights are encoded into the optical elements that light travels through, and the result arrives at a photodetector on the other side, where it gets converted back into a digital number. The multiplication happens as the light propagates. There is no clock grinding through it step by step, and the multiply itself costs almost no energy.The companies chasing this take noticeably different roads to the same idea. Lightmatter, the MIT spinout that has been at it longest, published the result that made the field look like computing rather than a physics demo: a Nature paper in April 2025 describing a six-chip package with four 128-by-128 photonic tensor cores that ran ResNet, BERT and an Atari-playing reinforcement-learning agent without retraining, at close to full 32-bit accuracy, delivering 65.5 trillion 16-bit operations per second on 78 watts of electrical and 1.6 watts of optical power. Lumai, out of Oxford, skips the waveguides altogether and does it in free space: a lens fans an input vector across a membrane whose transparency encodes the matrix, which lets it multiply matrices as large as 2,048 by 2,048 in a single pass. It launched its first server family, Iris, in April 2026, with an evaluation unit that runs Llama 8B and 70B in a hybrid setup. Neurophos in Austin raised a $110 million Series A in January, led by Gates Frontier with Microsoft’s M12 participating, for an optical processing unit that packs more than a million metamaterial modulators onto one chip, elements it says are ten thousand times smaller than earlier photonic components. Q.ANT in Stuttgart is building on thin-film lithium niobate and testing with the Jülich and Leibniz supercomputing centers. And in China, the LightGen prototype from Shanghai Jiao Tong and Tsinghua crammed more than two million photonic “neurons” into about 136 square millimeters and used them to generate and edit images entirely in light.Why this specific mix-up won’t go awayA few things stack on top of each other here. The vocabulary is the first one. “Post-silicon,” “beyond Moore’s law,” “computing with photons”; every one of those phrases has been used to sell quantum computing to investors for a decade, and photonic AI companies borrow the same language because they’re making a cousin of the same pitch: the old physics is running out, here’s new physics.The headlines are the second. Most of the “100x faster than Nvidia” stories are about narrow benchmarks, usually run against an A100, a GPU Nvidia launched in 2020, on tasks like image generation or classification where the prototype was designed to shine. LightGen’s own team describes it as proof that photonics can do real generative work, but only in tightly constrained domains. That nuance never survives the trip to the group chat.The third is that “photonic AI chip” genuinely means two different products. One kind computes with light. The other kind just moves data with light, replacing copper links between GPUs with optical ones, and that second kind is where the money is landing first. Lightmatter’s own public roadmap now centers on its Passage optical interconnect, with near-packaged optics deployments this year and co-packaged optics in 2027. So when someone says a photonics company is “in production with hyperscalers,” it’s worth asking whether the light is doing math or just carrying it.And the fourth is that the hype has already attracted the usual crowd. One Nasdaq micro-cap that started life as a pharmaceutical company, and whose filings earmarked it for cryptocurrency infrastructure, rebranded itself into photonic computing in September 2025. When a technology starts collecting those, people stop being able to tell the Nature papers from the ticker symbols.What it’s actually built to doThe specific claim these companies are making is about inference, and more precisely about the compute-heavy part of inference. Running a large model splits roughly into two phases: prefill, where the model chews through your whole prompt at once and is limited by raw arithmetic, and decode, where it emits tokens one at a time and is limited by how fast it can pull weights out of memory. Lumai is explicit that it’s going after prefill. That’s where a big optical matrix multiply pays off, because of a quirk of the physics: the energy cost of converting numbers into and out of light grows with the width of the vector, while the useful work grows with the square of it. Make the matrix bigger, and the efficiency improves, which is the opposite of how digital chips behave and the reason everyone in this field is obsessed with packing more optical elements into less space.What it isn’t built to do matters just as much. This is not a general-purpose replacement for a GPU. You can’t run arbitrary code on it. The non-linear parts of a neural network, the activation functions, normalization, the softmax inside attention, still get handed back to ordinary electronics. It doesn’t train frontier models. And because the light is an analog signal, it’s noisy: Lightelligence’s PACE platform averages around 7.6 bits of effective precision, and getting Lightmatter’s system to near-digital accuracy took careful calibration and a custom number format, not raw optics. Light also doesn’t solve the memory wall. If the bottleneck is moving weights out of memory, a faster multiplier doesn’t help, which is why decode-heavy workloads aren’t the target. These are limits by construction, not engineering shortfalls someone will patch next quarter.What it means for AI if it actually scalesThe honest framing of where AI compute is stuck is the same one you’ll hear about every alternative chip right now: the industry has been solving an energy problem by throwing more energy at it. Bloomberg has reported that nearly half of planned US data center projects will be delayed or cancelled this year, with electricity and electrical equipment cited as a primary reason. Photonic computing’s bet is that the single most common operation in AI was never a great fit for shoving electrons through transistors, and that light can do that one operation for a sliver of the energy. That’s a much narrower and more falsifiable claim than “we’re replacing Nvidia,” and I think that’s exactly why it’s more likely to be true. It doesn’t require new physics. The lasers are the same ones already shipping by the million for optical networking, and Lumai says it needs no new materials at all. What it requires is getting precision, conversion overhead, and packaging under control at scale, which is a hard but very ordinary kind of hard.If it works, the interesting consequence isn’t just cheaper inference. It’s that the compute-bound slice of AI inference, which today has one real hardware answer, buy more GPUs, gets a second answer built on different physics, at a moment when GPU supply and grid capacity are the two tightest constraints in the industry. The timelines are worth keeping honest, though. Lumai’s volume product is slated for 2028 and its follow-on for 2029, and Q.ANT is targeting series production in 2028. This is a claim about the 2028 data center, not next quarter’s.The irony I keep coming back to is that the first place light is winning big in AI isn’t replacing GPUs at all. It’s helping them talk to each other faster. In the near term, photonics makes Nvidia’s racks better before it makes them obsolete.I still don’t have a tidy one-liner for people who ask whether light-powered chips are about to kill the GPU. What I’ve settled on is something like: no, and they’re not quantum computers either, but the one piece of math that eats most of AI’s power bill might move into light, and that could matter more than either of those headlines.
