item.title: Levenza Launches Personal AI Agents for Enterprise With 300 Clients And Zero VC Funding
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: Personal AI agents became the breakout consumer technology of 2026. Meta's Muse reached 5 million US downloads in 22 days, against 56 days for ChatGPT, while Instinct raised $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation in September, a month after it was valued at $2.5 billion. The AI agents market is forecast to grow from $7.84 billion in 2025 to $52.62 billion by 2030, a rate of 46.3% a year.The office has been slower to catch up, even though the average worker now receives 117 emails and 153 Teams messages a day. Levenza, a San Francisco company that has signed more than 300 customers including Oliver Wyman, Goodwin and Hg Capital without raising outside capital, has made its personal AI agents available to enterprises worldwide. It has also acquired Fluid Inference, an applied AI lab, so that people can talk to their agents by voice.The Market for Personal AI AgentsInvestors and analysts expect agents to spread through business software at speed. Gartner expects 40% of enterprise applications to include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% in 2025, while the wider agents market is forecast to grow almost sevenfold by 2030 (our arithmetic). An AI agent, in plain terms, is software that does not stop at answering a question but goes on to take actions for a person, such as sending an invite or booking a room.Consumers showed how fast that idea can spread. Muse held the top spot among free iPhone apps in the US for 12 straight days, while Instinct's valuation rose about fourfold in roughly a month on the back of an agent that books travel, pays bills and makes calls for its users.Work is a harder setting for the same idea. A personal agent at home answers to one person, while an agent at a law firm or consulting firm has to deal with shared calendars, senior partners whose time comes first and executive assistants who handle requests for several people at once.The Coordination Problem at WorkMicrosoft's workplace data shows how much of the day now goes to coordination. The average worker receives 117 emails and 153 Teams messages a day, while the heaviest users are interrupted about 275 times a day, roughly once every two minutes. Nearly a third of meetings now span more than one time zone, up 8 points since 2021, while 57% of meetings are ad hoc calls without a calendar invite.Much of that load lands on assistants. There are about 3.5 million secretaries and administrative assistants in the US, including 489,300 executive assistants, while many professionals have no dedicated support at all and do their own scheduling between client work. Every hour spent chasing replies and moving meetings is an hour that a consultant, lawyer or banker does not spend on the work clients pay for.Where AI Returns Show Up FirstCompanies are under pressure to prove that their AI spending pays off. Only 13% of CIOs in a Gartner survey of 2,002 technology leaders said their organization had realized significant or transformational value from AI, while 58% said they face more pressure to deliver cost improvements from it.Admin work is one of the easiest places to measure a return, because the task is frequent, the time it takes is known and the result is either done or not done. Levenza users report saving up to three hours a day, which comes to about 690 hours a year over 230 working days, or roughly 17 working weeks. More than 95% of professionals using Levenza rate it highly, with many reporting feeling happier and less stressed at work.How Levenza's Agents WorkLevenza's agents run inside Teams, Slack and Outlook, so a firm does not have to adopt a new platform. A professional can ask in plain words for a client meeting to be arranged. The agent will then inspect calendars, coordinate with assistants, resolve conflicts and book the time. The agents also book rooms, liaise with travel agents, submit timesheets and keep each person's to-do list, picking up commitments from meetings, chats and email and working through open tasks in the background.Over time, each agent learns the preferences of the person it works for. Levenza's forward-deployed engineers, staff who work on site with each customer, adapt the agent to how each firm operates, including whose time takes priority and which requests go through an executive assistant. The company's website lists SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001 certifications, along with single sign-on and activity logs for enterprise control.Growth Without Venture CapitalLevenza has signed more than 300 customers, including Oliver Wyman, Kearney, Goodwin, Baird, Hg Capital and Spencer Stuart, while also securing multiple million-dollar enterprise contracts. It has grown profitably without raising outside capital, mostly through word of mouth with almost no marketing. Its net revenue retention is 170%, which means that customers who signed a year ago now spend 70% more in total, after any losses, while its gross revenue retention of 99% shows that almost no revenue walks out of the door.Those figures sit well above the norm for software companies. The median private business software company in SaaS Capital's 2025 survey of more than 1,000 firms reported net retention of 101% and gross retention of 91%, which puts Levenza 69 points and 8 points ahead. Retention at that level usually means that a product spreads inside a customer after it lands, as more partners, teams and offices ask for it.The Fluid Inference AcquisitionLevenza acquired Fluid Inference in September to build an agent that people can talk to as naturally as another person. The lab builds open-source models that hear, see, decide and speak, including FluidAudio, a speech toolkit for Apple devices that has trended at the top of GitHub. Its speech and system one models have been downloaded more than 4.7 million times and are used in more than 60 apps, including FluidVoice, VoiceInk and Spokenly. Fluid Inference was also a launch partner for NVIDIA's Nemotron speech models and has worked with Intel to bring speech and language models to AI PCs, while its founder Brandon Weng has joined Levenza as Head of Engineering.Voice is already part of the product. Someone driving to work can call their agent for a briefing on the day ahead, work through urgent emails and rearrange meetings without opening a laptop, or dictate directly into applications. Travel booking and expense management launch in 2027, widening the range of admin work professionals can hand over.Levenza grew out of Haefa Mansour's years at Bain, where she saw how much time professionals and executive assistants lost to routine coordination. Mansour, who holds a PhD from UC Berkeley, founded the company two and a half years ago with Austin Tackaberry, a former engineer at Databricks and Uber. She serves as its CEO.The pair chose to fund growth from customer revenue while much of the AI industry raised large venture rounds. That choice kept the company largely out of public view until this launch, with a business that was already profitable before its wider market debut.Levenza plans to build a network of agents that integrate deeply with enterprise systems and take ownership of larger goals, moving past single requests toward whole workflows. The long-term goal is a workplace where every professional has a personal agent, while executive assistants spend more of their time on the strategic work that depends on judgment and relationships.Consumer agents have shown how quickly people adopt AI that acts on their behalf. With hundreds of millions of people at work spending hours each week on coordination, the company that brings the same experience into the office has a market far larger than the one consumers opened up this year.Don’t forget to like and share the story!Vested Interest Disclosure: HackerNoon has reviewed the report for quality, but the claims herein belong to the author. #DYOR.

item.title: Anthropic's Safety-Conscious Corporate Culture Still Envisions Superintelligent AI
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
The Washington Post looks at Anthropic's "unique" corporate culture, where CEO Dario Amodei "leads his workforce through essays, long memos posted in Slack and twice-monthly all-hands talks jokingly known as 'Dario Vision Quests'...
"The CEO's output has established a constellation of beliefs treated as obvious, urgent and righteous inside the company: AI that supersedes humans is inevitable, the United States must limit China's AI development, and Claude might be conscious."
Inside this tight-knit culture, Anthropic staffers, who call themselves Ants, get to feel that they are working on the world's most urgent problems, with the smartest people, in a shared mission to safeguard humanity, according to interviews with more than a dozen people familiar with the company's ethos, including several current and former employees. At its core is a belief that Anthropic — and Amodei — know what's best for the world... "A pervasive thing at Anthropic is: We're going to put on our capes and we're going to be the responsible ones, and we're going to accrue great power, but ... because we're doing it responsibly, it's responsible to acquire more power," said a former employee who left the company this year and, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation from the company....
Its message to investors fit with a vision of the future that Amodei often sketches out for his staff, people familiar with the company said, in which AI companies have the power of nation-states. After nearly six years of telling his workers that powerful AI will force society's leaders to makep difficult decisions, Amodei is now one of the powers who must decide how to act, in a major test of the corporate culture he has created.... [Amodei] set out to create a more safety-conscious culture when he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with six people from his inner circle, most of them from OpenAI. In an internal memo the following year, Amodei laid out the stakes. "The current trajectory of AI development makes me think that there's a 20 to 30 percent chance that AGI will lead to the destruction or permanent stunting of humanity," he wrote, referring to the concept of artificial general intelligence, previously unreported court records show. He added that truly capable AI "seems more powerful/dangerous than nuclear weapons."
Amodei was careful about those he hired to work on that existential challenge. Recruits were screened with a "culture interview," even for back office and policy roles, according to former employees and an archived copy of the company's careers page... It's "a bit of an 'are you ready for the cult' interview," an Anthropic hiring manager texted the unsuccessful candidate, according to a screenshot reviewed by The Post...
Before ringing in Anthropic's record initial public offering at Times Square in New York on Thursday, Amodei delivered a short speech with some of his greatest hits. "To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control," Amodei said.

item.title: 48 Agent Skills Build MCP Servers, Claude Code Plugins and Even More Agent Skills
item.author: Interoperability in Software Publication
item.content:encoded: The fastest-growing category in agent tooling isn't skills that do your work. It's skills that help you build the tools: MCP servers that connect an agent to your systems, plugins that package your team's workflows, hooks that enforce your rules, and new skills that teach your agent what only your team knows.These 48 agent skills are for the builders. They come from Anthropic, Microsoft, Sentry, Cloudflare, Tech Leads Club, Jesse Vincent's Superpowers, Matteo Collina, Addy Osmani, Thomas Ricouard, Matt Pocock, Seth Hobson, Pramod Dutta and Daniel Avila's Claude Code Templates. All are MIT or Apache 2.0 licensed and packaged in Cuttlefish.MD, HackerNoon's license-checked library of SKILL.md files./plugin marketplace add hackernoon/cuttlefish-agent-skills /plugin install dev-workflow@cuttlefish /plugin install qa-testing@cuttlefish /plugin install security@cuttlefish /plugin install writing-blogging@cuttlefish For Codex, Cursor and other tools, clone the repo and copy the folders you want into your agent's skills directory.The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how agents talk to outside systems: your database, your ticket tracker, your internal APIs. Six skills for building and wiring up MCP servers. · Apache-2.0 · Dev Workflow pluginAnthropic's own guide to building MCP servers, and the best place to start. It runs in four phases: research and planning, implementation, review and testing, then writing evaluations. Its design advice is the useful part: balance full API coverage against task-level workflow tools, name tools with consistent prefixes like , return focused data with pagination, and write error messages that tell the agent what to try next. It recommends TypeScript, with Python's FastMCP as the alternative.Microsoft's adaptation of the same guide adds C# and .NET with Microsoft's MCP SDK alongside Python and TypeScript. Pick this one if your stack is .NET.A complete guide to FastMCP 3.0 for Python servers: tools, resources, authentication, providers, middleware and deployment.The other side of the connection: adding MCP servers to a Claude Code plugin through , choosing between stdio, SSE, HTTP and WebSocket transports, and using paths.A hybrid memory system exposed over MCP that gives agents persistent, searchable notes on architecture, patterns and decisions, so the next session doesn't start from zero.Teaches an agent to use the n8n-mcp tools well: finding nodes, validating configurations, using templates and managing n8n automation workflows.Write Skills That Write SkillsThe recursive section, and the one that matters most if you want an agent that does things your way. Ten skills for creating, testing, tuning and managing agent skills. · Apache-2.0 · Dev Workflow pluginAnthropic's skill for making skills, and the most complete. It drafts a skill, writes test prompts, runs them with and without the skill, shows you the results in a review viewer with quantitative benchmarks, and rewrites until you're happy. A separate step tunes the skill's description so it triggers when it should and stays quiet when it shouldn't. It also lets you skip the evals and just iterate by feel.Microsoft's version, aimed at skills for agents working with Azure SDKs and Microsoft Foundry. At 8,000 words it's the longest skill-authoring guide in the library. · Apache-2.0 · Writing & Blogging pluginSentry's approach treats skill writing as a pipeline: capture sources, synthesize them, do precision passes, author, register and validate. It can also improve an existing skill from examples of where it worked and where it didn't.Designs a new skill through a structured conversation. It triggers on phrases like "turn this into a skill" or "how do I teach my agent to do X," which is how most people actually ask.From Jesse Vincent's Superpowers. Its core idea, stated in bold: writing skills test-driven development applied to process documentation. Watch the agent fail without the skill, write the skill, confirm the agent passes, then refactor. It assumes you've read Superpowers' TDD skill first.Node.js core contributor Matteo Collina's skill for skills that aren't being used. It diagnoses "activation gaps," measures the difference in results with and without the skill, cuts context cost, tunes instruction salience and sets benchmark gates for releases.Scores a SKILL.md against the official specification and best practices across several dimensions, with concrete suggestions. Run it before you publish a skill for others.Thomas Ricouard's skill reads a project's past Codex sessions, memory files and existing skills, then recommends which new skills would pay off most and which existing ones have gone stale. Skill ideas grounded in what you actually do, not what you think you do.Addy Osmani's meta-skill governs how all the others are found and used. It runs at the start of a session and whenever the agent needs to decide which skill or workflow fits the task.Installs Codex skills into from a curated list or any GitHub repo path, including private repos.Skills are one piece of a plugin. These ten cover the rest of the kit.Creates and maintains Claude Code plugins with correct structure, and manifests, version bumps and marketplace integration. item.title: Your Event-Driven Architecture Is Running Fine... Until It Isn't
item.author: Stephen Tsoi
item.content:encoded: Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) is used in distributed systems to loosely couple applications. Instead of applications communicating directly with each other, they connect to a message broker and publish or consume events independently.However, loose coupling introduces a challenge that is often overlooked:How do you know your business process is actually working?The Monitoring Gap in EDAIn a traditional point-to-point design, the publisher can trigger an alert· if it cannot connect to the subscriber or· if the consumer does not acknowledge the request.The communication path is direct, so failures are usually visible.Applications connect to the message bus, not directly to each other, and the application disconnections are also normal scenarios, and the broker will store messages in the queue, so no messages are lost.From the broker's perspective, everything is operating as designed.The problem is that the business process may already be stalled.This makes monitoring one of the biggest operational challenges in EDA.Loose Coupling Does Not Mean Zero MonitoringOne of the major benefits of EDA is loose coupling, as "systems do not need to know about each other."From a design perspective, that's correct. From an operational perspective, it can be dangerous.Example 1: Fan-Out Control MessagesIf an upstream system fans out a control message to multiple downstream systems, it should know the status of each client to ensure data is synchronized across all systems. For example, a backend system sends a stop-sell or start-sell event to channel servers in different regions, and we need to ensure the event is successfully processed by all channel servers. Otherwise, it may impact business outcomes.Example 2: Stuck Consumer InstancesMultiple application instances may subscribe to messages from the same non-exclusive queue. If one of the instances crashes for any reason but does not exit properly, it may subscribe to messages without processing or acknowledging them to the broker. These messages can remain on the queue for a long time, causing message processing delays and wasting computing resources without doing any useful work.Monitoring Approach #1: Using APM for Multi-Factor AlertingMost brokers provide statistics at the VPN, queue, and client levels, and allow you to configure thresholds to trigger alerts. However, these alerts are usually based on fixed values and a single factor, making it difficult to meet flexible application requirements that depend on multiple factors. For example, a critical control message queue should trigger an alert when there are more than five spooled messages, and no client is bound to the queue.We can collect VPN, queue, broker, and client statistics through the management port every minute, and then use APM tools to generate alerts based on multiple conditions. For example, if a queue has more than five spooled messages and no client is bound to it, an alert can be triggered and sent to the corresponding team via email, Microsoft Teams, or WhatsApp if the condition occurs three times within ten minutes.Monitoring Approach #2: Application MetricsApplications should expose metrics for message publishing and consumption rates per second or per minute. If these numbers suddenly drop, an alert should be triggered for the operations or development team to investigate. In some cases, this may be a false alert.Monitoring Approach #3: Heartbeat EventsThe two monitoring approaches above focus on individual components rather than end-to-end message flow. How can we monitor the complete publisher-to-consumer flow?Establish a separate service that publishes heartbeat messages to a specific topic every five seconds, and have all queues subscribe to that topic. If a consumer does not receive a heartbeat within five seconds, it means something may be wrong, and an alert should be triggered.This solution is very simple, but it introduces additional traffic for heartbeat events, and consumers may experience performance impacts during traffic peaks.Each publisher sends a heartbeat event only when no messages have been published during the previous five seconds. Consumers process normal messages as usual and simply ignore heartbeat events.This solution provides end-to-end monitoring and does not impact consumer performance during peak traffic periods.EDA is a distributed architecture designed to loosely couple systems, but end-to-end process monitoring remains a significant challenge.Successfully publishing an event does not mean the business process completed successfully.Organizations typically adopt a combination of monitoring approaches:· Use APM tools to monitor broker and application health.· Monitor VPN, queue, broker, and client statistics to detect consumer issues.· Use heartbeat events to validate end-to-end message flows.There is no universal solution. The right approach depends on your business requirements, operational risk tolerance, and monitoring budget.One thing is certain: The more loosely coupled your architecture becomes, the more important observability becomes.How does your organization monitor event flow health in a large-scale EDA environment? Do you rely on broker metrics, application metrics, heartbeat messages, or a combination of all three? Share your experience in the comments.

item.title: Evaluating CNN Performance on CIFAR-10 Using ModelBrief
item.author: Chidiebere Njoku
item.content:encoded:
Machine learning initiatives often begin with rapid, engaging momentum. Sitting inside an interactive Jupyter notebook, an engineer can clean raw datasets, execute feature transformations, iterate on model architectures, tune hyperparameter grids, and watch validation metrics systematically improve. Within hours or days, an impressive prototype emerges, sparking immediate enthusiasm across product teams and organisational leadership eager to unlock AI-driven business value.Machine learning models can achieve impressive results during testing, but that does not always mean they are ready to be used in real-world applications. A model that performs well in a notebook may still have problems when deployed.These problems often become more noticeable when teams start working together. Data scientists may use different tools to track experiments, test results may be stored on individual computers, code may be scattered across different repositories, and preparing reports for reviews can take a lot of time.Things become even more difficult when a model starts producing unexpected results after deployment. Finding out what went wrong can be challenging, especially when there is no clear record of how the model was tested or what its performance looked like before deployment.This was one of the reasons I started building , an open-source Python library designed to make model evaluation easier, more consistent, and more transparent. It helps developers assess trained models, understand their performance, and produce clear reports without having to do everything manually.Understanding the Gaps in Machine Learning OperationsFor machine learning to be trusted and used reliably in organisations, four things are important: reproducibility, integrity, transparency and auditability. Teams need to be able to repeat their results, trust that their models and data have not been altered unexpectedly, understand how their models perform, and keep records that allow others to review and verify their work.When machine learning evaluation is not handled consistently, it can create several problems for organisations: Engineers often have to write separate scripts to calculate metrics, check errors and compare results across training, validation, and test datasets.Risk of breaking existing models: Some tools require changes to existing pipelines or retraining models, which can introduce unwanted changes to model behaviour or cause other parts of the system to fail.Difficulty understanding results: Raw numbers, charts and technical outputs can be difficult for non-technical teams, managers, and auditors to understand. Without clear and consistent evaluation reports, it becomes harder to investigate why a model's performance changed, compare results over time or provide evidence during audits and compliance reviews.Challenges of the Traditional Machine Learning WorkflowTo understand why traditional machine learning workflows struggle in large organisations, it helps to look at the different stages of model development and where problems tend to arise when there are no proper tools for evaluating models.Enterprise Business ImpactData scientists have to write new evaluation scripts for different experiments.Teams waste time repeating work, and different teams may use different ways to measure model performancePerformance results are collected manually and added to reports or presentations.This increases the chance of mistakes, slows down approvals and makes it harder to meet regulatory requirements.Moving models into production can involve complex dependencies on the tools used to train them.Models may be retrained when they shouldn't be, their saved weights may change, or information from the test data may accidentally influence the results.Important findings about model performance are often buried in notebooks and are difficult for others to access..Teams become dependent on individual developers to explain the results, making it harder to share knowledge and work together.Rethinking Model EvaluationTo address these challenges, I developed ModelBrief around a simple idea: once a machine learning model has been trained, its saved state should remain unchanged during evaluation. ModelBrief focuses on evaluating models after training. It does not train them again, change their weights, or require users to rebuild their existing machine learning workflows.The library works with different types of machine learning models, including Scikit-Learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. This means users can evaluate models built with different tools without having to change their existing setup. The main aim is to make it easier to understand how a trained model performs, identify areas that need attention, and produce useful evaluation reports without introducing extra complexity.Core Features of ModelBrief1. No Retraining or Model Changes: It evaluates an already-trained model without training it again or changing its internal settings. This means the model remains in its original state throughout the evaluation process.2. Works with Different Tools and Dependencies: It is designed to work with different machine learning frameworks and optional packages. If a particular extension or dependency is unavailable, it provides a clear warning instead of unnecessarily stopping the entire workflow.3. Different Ways to View and Share Results: Users can generate evaluation reports in different formats depending on their needs. These include simple summaries in the terminal, interactive HTML reports for exploring results, and PDF reports that can be shared with teams or used for documentation and reviewImplementing ModelBrief in Production WorkflowsInstallation & Environment SetupThe library installs modularly via standard Python package distribution channels. Specialized framework adapters can be included based on your active stack:# Core framework installation pip install modelbrief # Modular extensions for enterprise stacks pip install "modelbrief[xgboost]" # Gradient Boosting support pip install "modelbrief[pytorch]" # PyTorch integration wrappers pip install "modelbrief[vision]" # Computer Vision analytical suite pip install "modelbrief[ai]" # Optional AI narrative synthesis engine #Step 1: Multi-Split Execution Harness
#Integrating ModelBrief into existing training or pipeline scripts requires only a few lines of clean code. By passing the trained model alongside dataset partitions, you generate comprehensive multi-split evaluations instantly:
from modelbrief import ModelBrief from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
# 1. Train your estimator using standard workflow patterns model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42) model.fit(X_train, y_train)
# 2. Instantiate the ModelBrief evaluation harness across partitions audit = ModelBrief( model=model, X_train=X_train, y_train=y_train, X_val=X_val, y_val=y_val, X_test=X_test, y_test=y_test, ai=False # False by default and can be ) # 3. Export deterministic evaluation artifacts print(audit.show()) # Terminal summary for rapid debugging audit.html("reports/model_audit.html") # Interactive HTML web dashboard audit.pdf("reports/model_audit.pdf") # Governance PDF for compliance archiving Keeps the Original Model Unchanged: ModelBrief uses the trained model to make predictions without changing its internal settings. This ensures that the model remains the same before and after evaluation.-Compares Results Across Different Datasets: ModelBrief can evaluate a model using training, validation and test datasets. Comparing the results helps users identify problems such as overfitting, where a model performs well during training but struggles with new data.Step 2: Supporting Custom and Specialised ModelsNot all machine learning models are built in the same way. Some developers use custom neural networks, specialised data loaders, or their own prediction methods.To support these situations, ModelBrief allows developers to create their own adapters using the class. This provides a way to connect custom models to ModelBrief without changing how the original model is built or how its internal architecture works.import torch from modelbrief import ModelBrief, BaseAdapter
class PyTorchInferenceAdapter(BaseAdapter): """Custom adapter wrapping a PyTorch model for standardized evaluation."""
def predict(self, X): self.model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): tensor_input = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32) logits = self.model(tensor_input) predictions = torch.argmax(logits, dim=1) return predictions.numpy()
# Wrap custom model without altering its architecture or parameter states raw_pytorch_model = LoadCustomVisionModel() adapter = PyTorchInferenceAdapter(raw_pytorch_model)
# Run standardized audit across test set report = ModelBrief( model=adapter, X_test=test_tensor_data, y_test=test_labels, task="computer_vision" ) Understanding How the Adapter WorksConsistent Prediction Format: Different machine learning libraries handle predictions in different ways. ModelBrief provides a common format for these predictions, making it easier to work with models built using different tools.Separates Model Operations from Reporting: ModelBrief keeps the technical work happening inside a model separate from the tasks used to analyse and report its results. This means reporting tools receive information in a consistent format, regardless of how the original model was built.Optional Report ExplanationsModel evaluation can produce a lot of numerical results, graphs and tables. While these are useful to technical teams, they are not always easy for managers or other non-technical readers to understand. ModelBrief addresses this by offering an optional AI feature through . When users enable it by setting , the library uses the evaluation results to generate written explanations of model performance, highlight possible problems, and suggest areas that may need attention.This helps users understand what the results mean without having to interpret every table or graph themselves. The AI feature is optional. Users can still carry out model evaluation and generate reports without enabling it.Privacy-First AI PrinciplesExplicit Opt-in Infrastructure: External LLM calls are disabled by default (ai=False). Zero network requests or telemetry transmissions occur without explicit developer activation.Human-in-the-Loop Governance: AI-generated narratives serve as diagnostic baselines to support engineering reviews;final deployment decisions remain with qualified human specialists.Sample AI Diagnostic Output (Random Forest Evaluation)# Diagnostic Summary - Overall Performance:The estimator achieved a 1.00 ROC-AUC score on the test partition, primarily driven by Feature 2 (43.2% weight) and Feature 3 (42.8% weight). - **Overfitting Risk Alert: Perfect evaluation metrics combined with unconstrained default tree depth indicate potential overfitting to training distribution characteristics or latent data leakage.
# Recommended Remediation Steps 1. Cross-Validation Check:Run stratified k-fold cross-validation across raw data partitions to verify split integrity and eliminate leakage risks. 2. Hyperparameter Regularization: Restrict `max_depth` parameters and increase `min_samples_leaf` constraints to ensure robust generalization on out-of-distribution production inputs. Modelbrief supports different types of machine learning models and frameworks, most of which are:: Classification, regression, clustering and other traditional machine learning models.: Gradient boosting models for classification and regression.: Gradient boosting models designed for efficient training and prediction.: Gradient boosting models that work particularly well with categorical data.: Deep learning models and custom neural network architectures.: Deep learning models, including custom neural networks.: Neural network models built using the Keras API.!pip install modelbrief import tensorflow as tf from tensorflow.keras import layers, models
from modelbrief import ModelBrief
print("TensorFlow version:", tf.__version__)
(X_train, y_train), (X_test, y_test) = tf.keras.datasets.cifar10.load_data()# online dataset accessible for everyone
print("Dataset downloaded successfully.") print("Training images:", X_train.shape) print("Test images:", X_test.shape)
X_train = X_train[:300]# pick any number of images of your choice for training y_train = y_train[:300]
X_test = X_test[:60] #pick any number of image for testing y_test = y_test[:60]
# Convert labels from shape (n, 1) to (n,) y_train = y_train.flatten() y_test = y_test.flatten()
# Scale pixel values X_train = X_train.astype("float32") / 255.0 X_test = X_test.astype("float32") / 255.0
print("Training images:", X_train.shape) print("Test images:", X_test.shape)
model.fit( X_train, y_train, epochs=25, batch_size=20, verbose=1 )
print("CNN trained successfully.")
report = ModelBrief( model=model, X_test=X_test, y_test=y_test, ai=True )
print(report.show())
report.html("tensorflow_cnn_report2.html")
report.pdf("tensorflow_cnn_report2.pdf")
print("HTML and PDF reports created successfully.") In the report above, ModelBrief documented a non-retrained Keras classifier (79,530 parameters) evaluated on 60 CIFAR-10 test images across 10 classes. It recorded 23.33% accuracy (23.78% balanced accuracy), 0.7937 ROC-AUC, 46 misclassifications, a 10x10 confusion matrix showing frequent errors across classes such as 0 and 6, with AI explanations and remediation steps.Insights into Better Machine Learning PracticesHaving a consistent way to evaluate machine learning models using makes a big difference in how data science and engineering teams work together. By providing a consistent way to evaluate models, generate reports and share results without retraining, ModelBrief helps reduce repetitive work, simplify auditing, avoid unnecessary changes to trained models and make evaluation findings easier for teams to access and understand."Making Information Easier to Share: Automatically generating PDF and HTML reports gives teams a clear record of how their models perform. Product managers, risk teams, and software engineers can all review the results and understand where a model performs well and where it needs improvement.Making Deployment Faster and Easier: Automating reports allows teams to include model checks in their existing CI/CD processes. This helps identify problems such as changes in data, imbalanced datasets or declining model performance before a model goes live.Improving the Way Teams Work: Relying less on manual checks in notebooks makes model evaluation more consistent. Teams can follow the same process, keep records of their results and make it easier to review models as projects grow. Having clear and easy-to-understand reports helps teams make better decisions about their models. Instead of relying only on accuracy scores, they can look at the full results, understand where mistakes are happening and decide what needs to be improved before putting a model into use.Saving Time and Reducing Repeated Work: By bringing different evaluation results together in one place, ModelBrief reduces the need for developers to write the same scripts or prepare reports manually for every project. This gives them more time to focus on building, testing and improving their machine learning solutions.Building a successful machine learning model involves more than achieving a high accuracy score. Organisations also need to understand how their models perform, keep track of changes, and make sure they can be properly tested before and after deployment. This is the problem that ModelBrief aims to address. By separating model evaluation from the training process, it provides an open-source tool that helps developers, researchers, and organisations evaluate their trained models and produce clear reports. The goal is to make machine learning evaluation easier, more consistent and accessible to people working with different tools and frameworks.

item.title: Best Developer Tools for PR Testing in 2027: Building an Agentic Dev Stack
item.author: QA.tech
item.content:encoded: Coding agents open pull requests faster than anyone can review them, and the review queue is now the slow part of shipping. The question is how to confirm each change works without burning out the people who test it. The best PR testing setup for 2027 checks every change at three points:inside the coding tool, before the PR is createdbefore merge on PR’s preview deploymentThis guide covers the tools at these three checkpoints, their cost and what they can miss. It is written for engineering and product teams with a high release cadence, where more and more features come from coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. Let your coding agent check its own work while it builds, but take the merge verdict from something else. On every PR, run an AI code reviewer on the diff and an independent test on the running preview. After merge, keep a small pinned set of critical flows running on main and in production. Everything else gets dynamic testing scoped to what each diff touches.Why Is Verification the Bottleneck Now?Confirming that a change works is now the slowest step in the delivery pipeline. CircleCI’s 2026 State of Software Delivery shows that average daily workflow runs rose 59% YoY, while main-branch success rate fell to ~70% (CircleCI). Developers report the same thing. In the 2026 Stack Overflow survey, nearly half said they trust AI output only when they can verify it, and 6.6% trust it for important decisions (Stack Overflow).None of this started with AI. Scripted regression suites were slow and brittle long before coding agents. Agents simply multiply the number of changes those suites have to judge.There is also a question of independence. Coding agents write good code and plenty of unit tests, but those tests share the agent’s assumptions. If the agent misread the ticket, its tests misread it too, and both pass.What Does an Agentic Dev Stack Look Like?The stack has three checkpoints. Each checkpoint is based on a different question, so each requires different tools.While the agent works, before a PR existsDoes the change build and behave locally?Linters, type checkers, unit tests, Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools MCP, QA.tech MCP serverWhen a PR opens or updatesIs the diff sound, and does the preview work for a user?CodeRabbit, Greptile, Copilot code review, Cursor Bugbot, Vercel, Netlify, QA.tech, QA Wolf, MomenticOn main, staging and productionDid the release break a critical flow?Pinned regression suite, scheduled smoke runsInner Loop: Checks Before the PR ExistsLinters, type checkers and the agent’s own unit tests run in seconds. Agents should run them on every iteration.Some tools give the agent a browser to work with while it debugs. Two examples:Playwright MCP, from Microsoft, uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to let an agent drive a real browser.Both help the agent see what it broke. Neither keeps a test suite, so nothing they do runs again on the next change.QA.tech’s MCP server connects Claude Code, Cursor or Codex to its QA agents. From inside the coding tool, your agent can:start a run of existing testsadd a test described in plain Englishopen a tunnel so the QA agents can test before anything is committed inner loop checks are evidence the agent gathers for itself. They shorten iteration, but they should not be the merge verdict.PR Gate: Review the Diff, Then Test the PreviewReview bots catch logic slips, risky patterns and convention drift before a human opens the PR.Rough monthly cost (10 developers, 200 PRs)Per developer: $24, $48 or $72 per month (annual billing)About $240 on the entry planStandards enforcement across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps$1 per credit, no seat fee; a Base review is 1 credit, Plus 3, Apex 10About $200 at Base depth, $600 at PlusCross-file bugs in large codebasesUsage-based, $1.00 to $1.50 per average runAbout $200 to $300 at one run per PR; new pushes can trigger more runsTeams that write code in CursorAI Credits plus GitHub Actions minutesVaries; GitHub publishes no fixed per-review priceTeams already paying for CopilotAll four share one limit: they just read the diff without opening the app. The AI code review roundup compares them in more depth.Vercel, Netlify, Render, Railway and Fly.io can deploy every PR to its own URL. When connected to GitHub, they register a GitHub Deployments record that testing tools pick up automatically. each preview needs seed data. test users must be able to sign in. protected previews need a bypass so the testing tool can reach them. extra environments cost money.If you have no previews, you can test after merge against staging instead.PR previews, staging, productionAgent context and a small pinned suiteAn independent verdict on every PR at high volumeChromium-based web only; native mobile on simulators and emulatorsLittle, since their team can own the suiteDeterministic Playwright code and managed coverageLess scoped to each PR’s diffYAML tests and CI wiring in your repoTests reviewed alongside the codeThe agent that wrote the change also writes its testFull control, open source, Chromium, Firefox and WebKitFlake triage and upkeep are yoursThe QA agent reads the PR description, the linked Jira or Linear ticket and the diff.It works out which user flows the change can affect.It selects existing tests that cover those flows and writes new ones only where coverage is missing.It sets test depth by blast radius, so a small change to payments gets more scrutiny than a large change to an isolated settings page (how risk is scored).The QA agents open the preview in a browser and work toward a user goal from what is on the screen rather than replaying fixed selectors, so tests adapt when the UI changes. Choosing the tests from each change and running them against the live app is what QA.tech calls dynamic testing: it answers whether the product still works for a user once the change is in. A code reviewer answers whether the diff looks right; this is the other half.After merge, run a small pinned regression set on main and on a schedule against production. Cover only the flows that must never break, such as sign-up, login and payments. For compliance-critical journeys, pin them to explicit steps that fail loudly with full traces, inside the same platform.You do not need to rebuild an old suite one to one. On GitHub, a post-merge step can promote tests a PR review created into the regression suite. Scheduled exploratory testing covers the long tail. Findings land in Slack, Jira or Linear.What Slips Through Each Checkpoint?No one checkpoint covers every row. That is the case for running all three.Logic bug visible in the diffCode looks right, but the flow breaks in a browserSometimes, with the ticket linkedCaught when the ticket is linkedPreview and production configs differBackend side effect invisible in UI or APIWhen Is a DIY Playwright Stack the Better Choice?Sometimes plain Playwright is the right call. It makes sense when:you have a handful of stable flowsyou need the Firefox or WebKit enginesauditors want tests as code in your repoyour engineers have time to own the suiteThe cost is ownership. Someone maintains the tests, the CI wiring and the flake triage, plus the model bill if an agent writes the tests for you.Whatever you choose, people keep the judgment calls. QA agents take over repetitive verification. Your team still decides on risk, usability and the merge itself, and the PR checklist shows how to split those duties.If you’d rather not build and maintain the preview-testing flow yourself, QA.tech runs PR testing with QA agents on GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps.
